extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students solving polynomial/trinomial equations (readers of The Mathematician)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical trigonometric-logarithmic method for approximating complex (unreal) roots of trinomial numerical equations by representing a root in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ), deriving equations for r and θ, and solving numerically (via logarithms and bracketing/interpolation).

rubrics_metrics.name: assume root in polar form
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the unknown x = r(cos θ + √−1 sin θ) (with r real, θ between 0° and 90°), so that x^m = r^m(cos mθ + √−1 sin mθ), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational representation for the method; choosing this form converts the trinomial into separate real and imaginary equations. (Verbatim phrasing from text: 'assumption of a (the unknown) = r(cos 9 + +/—] sin@)'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: equate real and imaginary parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute the polar form into az^m + bz^n + c = 0 and equate real and imaginary parts to obtain two real equations: ar^m cos mθ + br^n cos nθ + c = 0 and ar^m sin mθ + br^n sin nθ = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat r^m and r^n as unknowns to be solved from these two simultaneous equations (these are displayed as (3) and (4) in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: choice of which equation to use for r (parity rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If m is even, use equation (4) to compute r (to avoid ambiguity in sign); if n is even, use equation (3); if both odd either may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text guidance: 'Should m be even, we must, to avoid ambiguity in sign, use (4), but if 2 be even, then (3) must be used. If both m and n be odd, then of course either (3) or (4) may be employed.' This avoids sign-ambiguity when extracting r from sine/cosine relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: eliminate r to obtain θ-equation (logarithmic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate r^m and r^n between the two equations to obtain an equation in θ alone of the form given in (5), which is then solved by taking logarithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equation (5) relates powers of sines of multiples of θ and coefficients; the practical step is to take logarithms of both sides so numerical tables can be used. The author notes: 'since I take the logarithm of each side of (5), it makes very little matter whether the coefficients a, b, c be large or small numbers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: sign-handling for sine terms when RHS negative
rubrics_metrics.description: If the right-hand member of the θ-equation is negative, exactly one of sin(mθ) or sin(nθ) must be negative; replace the negative sine by −sin(angle − 180°) to work with positive sine-table values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: 'Since the right hand member of this equation is essentially negative, one and one only of the two, sin 3θ, sin 7θ must be negative. When the latter is negative, write −sin(7θ − 180°) ...' Also: when a sine appears in an even power it may be treated as positive (e.g., 'since sin 100 enters (6), in an even power, we may, in every case, treat sin 100 as a positive quantity, whether it be so or not').

rubrics_metrics.name: interval bracketing and use of Double Position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trial evaluations to bracket θ in a small interval and then apply the rule of Double Position (interpolation) to refine θ to minutes/seconds accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author guidance: 'On the whole, I am inclined to think that the rule of Double Position is best adapted to find the values of θ.' The worked example shows bracketing θ between integer degrees, evaluating the θ-equation at endpoints, then interpolating proportionally to obtain minutes and seconds, and iterating to desired precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: treat even powers and sign-ambiguity carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When trig functions appear in even powers treat their sign as effectively positive in the power; ensure correct choice of shifted-angle for negative sine factors to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit note: '...we may, in every case, treat sin 100 as a positive quantity, whether it be so or not.' Also the parity-based choice of (3) vs (4) reduces sign ambiguity when solving for r.

rubrics_metrics.name: compute r once θ known, then obtain quadratic real factor
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding θ, compute r from the appropriate equation (3) or (4); then r cos θ and r sin θ give the complex pair r(cos θ ± i sin θ), and the corresponding real quadratic factor is x^2 − 2r cos θ x + r^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text shows explicit computation steps using logarithms and trig-table values; it emphasizes computing log r, then r cos θ and r sin θ, and assembling the quadratic factor (example yields quadratic factors like x^2 − 2.028034 x + 1.454561).

rubrics_metrics.name: practical remarks on numerical labour and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Using common logarithmic and trigonometric tables suffices; the numerical labour for finding one pair of unreal roots is nearly the same regardless of the degree of the trinomial, and only small multipliers (1/2, 2, m−2) typically arise in logarithmic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author commentary: 'the number of figures that can be obtained by our common logarithmic and trigonometric tables ... is indeed limited, but the extent to which the approximation can be carried by means of these will, I doubt not, be found amply sufficient... the only multipliers 1/2, 2, and m−2 will always be small... the actual labour required to determine a single pair of unreal roots is nearly the same, and thus the work necessary to determine all the roots will be nearly proportional to the degree of the equation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: example-driven verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify each computational step by working a full example (e.g., x^10 + 22x^3 − 5 = 0): bracket θ values, refine, compute r, then construct quadratic factors and collect all conjugate pairs to factor the trinomial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text includes a detailed worked example demonstrating bracketing, interpolation, logarithmic computation of r, and assembly of four quadratic factors; follow a worked example to ensure correct sign handling and arithmetic.
